title: Data lake, lakehouse or warehouse?

rows.label: In one line
values: Raw files in cheap storage, given a structure when read
Tables made of open files, with transactions
A managed database built for analytics

rows.label: Where the data lives
values: Your object storage, in any format: JSON, CSV, Parquet, images
Your object storage, as Parquet files tracked by a table format
The warehouse’s own managed storage, in its own format

rows.label: Schema
values: Applied on read; nothing checks data on the way in
Enforced on write; columns can change without rewriting files
Enforced on write

rows.label: Updates and deletes
values: No transactions: rewrite the affected files yourself, and hope no reader catches you halfway
Atomic commits; `MERGE`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` through the engine
Built in

rows.label: Who can read it
values: Any engine that reads the files, each with its own table definitions unless they share a catalog
Any engine that speaks the table format, through a shared catalog
Mainly the warehouse’s own engine

rows.label: Data it suits
values: Anything, including images, audio and documents
Tables, with other files kept alongside them
Tables and semi-structured JSON

rows.label: What you operate
values: Storage is easy; keeping the lake findable and trustworthy is the real work
Catalog, compaction, snapshot expiry and permissions, unless a platform manages them
Little: tuning, compaction and access control are managed

rows.label: Cost at scale
values: Object-storage prices; engines cost money only while they run
Object-storage prices; engines cost money only while they run
Storage and compute priced by the vendor

rows.label: Reach for it for
values: Cheap raw storage, and files that aren’t tables
One copy of data shared by BI, ML and streaming
Quick BI wins with a small team

tip: They stack more than they compete. A lakehouse is a data lake with a table format on top, and most warehouses now read and write Iceberg tables in it. Ask where the authoritative copy lives, whether writes are transactions, and who else can read it without a copy job.
